dossier.public_summary: The light-curve shows five dips with very different depths (one about twice the others) and odd-even dips differ significantly, which is the signature of a stellar eclipse at half the quoted period rather than a planet. The star is also a fast rotator with spot variability near the 10.8-day period and only a weak, inconsistent signal. This is best explained as a false alarm or on-target/eclipsing binary, not a transiting planet.

reasons.why: Five transits are wildly inconsistent (chi2=70.19371024958429 dof=4). One at btjd 3206.367 is 6906 ppm (4.7 sigma above mean) while two others are 258 and 354 ppm (4.5 and 4.1 sigma below). The top three carry 0.998 of the signal.

Odd depths 4860 ppm vs even 2345 ppm differ by 0.5176 depth_ratio 2.1 with 3.8 sigma significance, with depth_difference_ppm 2516. Combined with the large transit-to-transit scatter this is best explained as a stellar eclipse at twice the period (7.0 d? ) rather than a planet at 10.8 d.

Star shows a strong 8.979 d rotation in sector 69 (amplitude 6607 ppm, false_alarm 0.00015272222145647424) close to the 10.8386 d signal period (~1.207x, not an exact multiple). A dip at a multiple of the spin is expected to show stellar-warped shape or phase curve; here the shape is flat (v_sigma -3.497) but the huge spot modulation and inconsistent depths point to variable eclipses/false alarm.

Differences imaging cannot locate the dip (why: no sector with a clear difference image, sector 69 diff_snr 2.3 used false). No on-target centroid, so a blended NBEB cannot be ruled out, and plausible_within_1px=0 only rules out 25%-eclipse neighbours within one TESS pixel (21 arcsec), not an off-pixel blend.

ML planet score 0.17 is well below median planet (0.5) and below the 0.1 threshold where false positives dominate, consistent with the inconsistent depths and odd/even difference arguing against a planet.
